source: It's just like a chess game, you see. First your turn, then mine, then yours, then mine, and so on, and so forth.
Lady Simona merely granted you the human seat at the board. You inherited her match!
And let me tell you, in the past she's made some rather atrocious moves.
So all of this is just spectacle to you.
That's right, isn't it? That's what all of this is. It's just a performance you're putting on.
In that case, I'll never make a decision. You cannot force my hand.
Right now, I choose to stay in Elsinore.
Heh... heh. Heh... heh...
Hah hah hah hah hah! How clever!
Wrong call, Ophelia.
This is your last chance to be reasonable.
Give me the Book, or suffer an eternal hell in a prison I've designed especially for you.
Do you think this little game I've put you in is the worst it can be? Oh, no, dearest...
It can be far worse still.
I alone can understand the details of your pain, for I have seen it all...
This match we're in, Ophelia... you and I... it's like playing with a child.
Your strategy lacks efficacy; your designs are impotent. I will ensnare you every time. Don't you understand?
You will linger here, undying, growing bored and stupid and slow. Just like King Hamlet before you.
I've told you I won't give you the Book. Leave me.
Leave you? I am Elsinore. I am the eye in every wall and my fingers run through every flagstone. I can no more leave you than you can leave me!
And my dear, you can never truly leave me. Even when the Book is back in my hands. I will always linger.
And while you're here, I will dismantle you piece by piece. I will not allow you to find more than the smallest happiness.
I will smother you until every shred of your flesh is ground beneath my toes.
Yes. That's the face I came to see.
I hope to be seeing more of it very soon...
'Til then, Ophelia.
This isn't over. This cannot be over. There must be a way to stop him.
My lord Hamlet! What an odd occasion to come across you here.
Odd, you say? These days the very walls seem to sing my name... now that's odd.
I... er, don't understand, my lord. What do you mean?
I'm sure you think you're being very coy accosting me here, my lady Brit. And yet!
I see right through your womanly act. You feign concern for me, but there's something more in it.
I was merely curious to see your, ahem, strange condition up close.
Well, then. Oughtn't you to come a little closer?
Ah... my lord, it isn't proper.
How are you to assess my condition, then, if you won't even look into my eyes?
Or test my sanity via some other method, then. Take my hand, and see if I flinch. Sing to me, and see if I sit quietly. Kiss me, and see if my heart is stirred.
Er... my lord... I think I ought to take my leave of you.
So be it, then. Your errant behavior is most strange to me, Lady Brit.
(The man's absolutely mad. Ophelia was right.)
(Ergh. Lock him up and throw away the key, that's what I think!)
(S-still, there is a certain attractive air about him, though...)
Gentlemen. Can I get you a drink?
We've come fer our coin, 'n fact.
Aye. We're here to collect what yeh owe.
Before the lord come the barking hounds, I suppose.
Can that master not come to see me himself?
I've told him I'd pay him. And when I have the coin, I intend to keep my word.
The Danish King has squeezed every coin from my pockets in tax to fuel his lavish wedding.
He's a rich man, and I a poor one. That's the way of the world. I've nothing to give you yet.
Can we not settle this reasonably?
One day, Othello. That's what yeh get.
Today we've given yeh early warning.
Tomorrow we'll be less kind.
...I see.
So you have no reasonable intent whatsoever. Merely the thuggish rallying cry of 'more coin!'
And you intend to brutalize me regardless... as if I could grind gold out of the stones in the floor of this old inn.
Words, words, words. That's all yeh got.
How about bein' a man of yer word?
Wah hah hah!
Go. Get out.
What's going on here?
Guard captain.
Nothin', sir! We wos just coming around for a drink...
That's not what I've heard from the good Lady Ophelia here.
Leave, and never return, or I'll have my men rout out all of you and clean the back alleyways until they sparkle.
T-thank you, sir.
Don't thank me. Thank Lady Ophelia.
Now. Was I sufficiently intimidating?
I think so. With any luck, they won't return.
I owe you a great debt, my lady. You are as noble-hearted as you are beautiful.
While I wish I could pay you, all I have to offer are my stories.
I would love to spin you a tale in private, have you the time to listen.
This evening at midnight, I close the bar. Perhaps you could meet me then?
...Say, we've been drinking all day.
Haven't we earned a tall tale?
So you only patronize my tavern for the stories I tell?
Come, friends. You offend me. My ale's at least twice as good as the horse piss in the alley outside.
And besides, you only want to hear a tale so you can doze off at my tables.
Tell the one about the sea-witch!
Yeah, that old evil hag!
Ha—so be it, then.
...Now, friends. As you may recall, I was a haggard sailor in my youth...
And I spent my years in servitude to many captains, some good, and some evil, but all greedy.
Now, it so happens that in the middle of a mysteriously stormy summer, our ship the Titania was called upon for a private mission.
We were invited to the glistening palace of the Sultan himself, and landed on the coast of Algiers soon after.
There were women from his harem there to greet us, gilded and sinuous, clad all in white.
And wine was poured, and we were plied with sweet music and song for all the long night.
Get to the part with Sycorax!
Patience, friend. Patience!
The Sultan himself begged us to take a certain... 'problem' off his hands. A murderous witch, but a pregnant one.
The vile witch Sycorax had committed numerous bloody crimes against the Sultan, and for that, he wanted her banished. He could not kill a woman with child, he said.
He asked our crew to take her to an island far from his shores and leave her there forever, for magic cannot travel over the ocean.
In return, we were each offered a mountain of gold; enough to last us seven lifetimes over, if not more, as wealthy men.
Then... we saw her. The witch.
Was she uglier than a goat?
The blue-eyed hag... she defies description.
The first time she came aboard our ship in chains, we could see she was heavily with child. She stared at me, and I knew she could see all my thoughts laid bare.
We pushed out from the Sultan's port that day and set sail. We chained her in the hold. Two suns later, our captain died suddenly in the night.
The men whispered that she had cursed him. But who were we to say? After all, the captain loved his rum and often drank to uselessness. This time he'd simply gone too far.
...But by the time we had reached the Mediterranean, one man had gone insane and jumped overboard, and one man had slit another's throat, then his own.
Now I had become the ship's captain, by the crew's vote.
Wait a minute.
Wasn't that island in the New World before?
You're telling it differently!
Useless details of no consequence.
I went to visit the witch myself. She sat in the darkness of the hold, her hair limp, her eyes haggard, her gaze poison.
'Witch,' I told her, 'I will free you from your chains and give you my cabin if you kill no more of my men.'
At that, she merely laughed. 'And what will I do then to entertain myself? You must give me something better.'
So I gave her all I had.
'If you leave my men alive,' I said, 'I will tell you one story each night, until we land on the island's shores.'
She laughed again. But in the end, she consented. And I spent every night telling her long tales, just as I sit here now, keeping her enthralled.
True to her word, no more of my men died. But when we approached shore, we were beset with a violent storm. The ship railed so wide on the waves I thought we would certainly perish.
Rain and hail pummeled us through the darkness as I maintained course. The lamps had all been sodden. Only lightning briefly lit our path forward, followed by screaming thunder.
At last I saw land, a hundred meters out.
And suddenly—out of nowhere—craggy rocks rose into the air. We were going to hit rock! We were going to drown! The ship shuddered and screeched.
As men flew overboard, I heard their dying screams. And as I looked at the bow of the ship... I saw Sycorax.
Sycorax was laughing. Standing at the bow of the ship, unaffected by rain or the jerk of the now-dead ship. Just laughing, and laughing, and laughing.
I ran to her and grabbed her by the shoulders. 'Witch,' I screamed, 'You must save us from this hell!'
She looked at me then. The rain ceased. The waters calmed. The ship stabilized. And she smiled.
'You alone showed me kindness,' she said to me. 'This island belongs to me now. Begone, and take your life as your due reward.'
...And then I awoke.
You... awoke?
I was covered in sand, lying on the shore of a mysterious beach. It was day, and the sun heated my back. I'd been there for God knows how long.
As I crawled up onto the shore, I saw the white tip of the Sultan's palace breaking the treeline. I was in Algiers.
I tried to tell him what I'd seen, but with no ship and no crew, he assumed I'd gone mad and deserted my men. He wouldn't hear my tale.
With no gold, no ship, and no crew, I left Algiers on foot. But I never forgot the blue-eyed hag, or the gift she gave to me.
God's blood, what time is it?
We've been here all day.
The missus is waiting. I've got to go.
Til next time, friends.
The poor soul sat singing by a tree, sing all a green willow...
Her hand on her bosom, her head on her knee...
The fresh streams ran by her, and murmur'd her moans...
Her salt tears fell from her, and soften'd the stones...
Sing willow, willow, willow.
Apologies, my lady. I forgot myself. Can I get you something to drink?
No, I was merely listening. It's a sad song, isn't it? A song about hopelessness.
